reading.title: Children of Time
reading.author: Adrian Tchaikovsky
reading.note: It’s hard sci-fi about how a non-human intelligence evolves, and it’s pure enjoyment that still makes you think.

want.title: The Art of Doing Science and Engineering
want.author: Richard Hamming
want.why: This one is about choosing problems that matter and building judgment over a career. Read it first.

want.title: The Inner Game of Tennis
want.author: W. Timothy Gallwey
want.why: It’s the best book I know on performing freely instead of supervising yourself. It applies directly to dance, piano and boxing, and to chess, where you think too long over moves.

want.title: The Brain from Inside Out
want.author: György Buzsáki
want.why: Buzsáki argues against the outside-in view of perception, and argues it well. It has real substance, not pop science.

want.title: Surfing Uncertainty
want.author: Andy Clark
want.why: It covers prediction, action and embodiment at a level that should hold your attention.

want.title: A Mind at Play
want.author: Jimmy Soni & Rob Goodman
want.why: Shannon did serious work and played seriously too, with juggling, chess and gadgets. It’s a useful model for not separating the two.

want.title: The Rider
want.author: Tim Krabbé
want.why: It’s a short novel set entirely inside one road race, and you can read it in an afternoon.

want.title: Stoner
want.author: John Williams
want.why: It’s a quiet novel about a life lived on its own terms, with all the costs that brings.

want.title: The Brothers Karamazov
want.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky, translated by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky
want.why: It deals with free will, faith, fathers and sons. It’s long, and it’s worth it.

want.title: High Output Management
want.author: Andy Grove
want.why: It’s the operating manual for when you eventually run a team or a company.
